summary: This informational document provides a framework overview of the DetNet Controller Plane, covering concepts and requirements that could underlie a future solution specification. It does not itself define a protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: DetNet promises messages arrive on time. This describes the controller that sets that up, as a first sketch.

subtitle: Framework for controlling deterministic networks that guarantee delivery timing.

tldr.problem: Deterministic networks need to guarantee low packet loss and maximum end-to-end delivery latency, but require a control plane to set this up across diverse network topologies.
tldr.mechanism: The controller plane instantiates flows, allocates resources, computes explicit paths, manages label distribution, and monitors network performance using either distributed protocols, a centralized controller, or both.
tldr.outcome: Networks can reserve bandwidth, buffer space, and compute resources to meet service-level agreement requirements for real-time applications.

facts.label: DetNet goal
facts.value: Extremely low packet loss with assured maximum end-to-end latency

facts.label: Core functions
facts.value: Flow instantiation, resource reservation, path computation, monitoring

today: RFC 9938 is an Informational RFC that provides a framework for future DetNet Controller Plane protocol work. It has not been obsoleted and is referenced in ongoing DetNet standardization efforts.

sections.title: What is Deterministic Networking
sections.content:
Deterministic Networking (DetNet) provides the ability to carry data flows for real-time applications with extremely low packet loss rates and assured maximum end-to-end delivery latency. The data plane defines how packets are forwarded, but the controller plane is responsible for setting up and maintaining the flows, allocating network resources, and distributing the configuration information to network nodes.

This document is a framework, not a protocol specification. It outlines what a DetNet Controller Plane must do and discusses three architectural approaches (distributed, centralized, and hybrid) without specifying the exact protocols or detailed mechanisms. Future work will define the actual protocols for implementing these functions.
sections.plainLanguage: Real-time applications need networks where messages always arrive on time. The controller is the part that makes sure the network is set up to deliver.

sections.title: Controller Plane Responsibilities
sections.content:
The DetNet Controller Plane combines what are normally separate control and management plane functions. The control plane side handles instantiation and modification of flows, label allocation and distribution (in MPLS networks), and active signaling to support DetNet functions. The management plane side handles performance monitoring, connectivity verification, fault management, and testing of replication and elimination functions.

Key responsibilities include dynamically creating, modifying, and deleting DetNet flows; supporting flow aggregation; managing explicit paths that do not change with network topology changes; reserving resources such as bandwidth, buffer space, and processing capacity; specifying queuing disciplines; and monitoring whether flows meet their service-level agreement (SLA) requirements for latency and packet loss.
sections.plainLanguage: The controller keeps track of all the messages flowing through and makes sure each one gets the resources it needs, like a ticket-taker on a train that reserves seats and checks that everyone arrives on time.

sections.title: Control Plane Architectures
sections.content:
The framework describes three possible architectures. In a fully distributed approach, network nodes use distributed signaling protocols (such as RSVP-TE for MPLS networks) to propagate flow information through the network. Each node makes local decisions based on topology information. This avoids a single point of failure but requires protocol extensions for DetNet-specific features.

In a fully centralized approach, an SDN controller collects topology and capability information from network nodes, receives flow requests, computes optimal paths, and configures devices using protocols such as NETCONF or YANG. This provides global path optimization but creates a potential single point of failure.

A hybrid approach combines both methods, with a controller computing paths and distributing them to edge nodes, which then use signaling protocols to establish labels and resources. This balances the benefits and drawbacks of both approaches.
sections.plainLanguage: Three ways to do it: every router decides its own path, one central planner tells everyone what to do, or a planner suggests paths that routers then execute.

sections.title: DetNet-Specific Mechanisms
sections.content:
Explicit paths are essential because DetNet flows must follow stable paths that do not change when network topology changes. The controller plane must compute paths that meet SLA requirements (bandwidth, maximum delay, delay variation, loss ratio) and then establish those paths in the network.

Resource reservation allocates not just bandwidth but also buffer space and queue management resources to protect DetNet flows from congestion. The controller learns what resources a flow needs from its traffic specification, which describes worst-case traffic (interval between packets, maximum packets per interval, maximum packet size).

PREOF support enables packet replication and duplicate elimination for redundancy. The controller must compute and establish multiple paths (multiple Label Switched Paths in MPLS) from replication points to elimination points and maintain the mapping of DetNet flows to path segments.
sections.plainLanguage: The controller picks a fixed route for important messages, reserves seats and buffering space for them, and can make backup copies that go different ways.

sections.title: Different Network Technologies
sections.content:
DetNet can operate over different underlying technologies. In MPLS networks, the controller distributes Service Labels (S-Labels) and Aggregation Labels (A-Labels) using protocols like LDP, RSVP-TE, or BGP, with extensions for DetNet-specific functions.

In IP networks, the DetNet data plane is simpler than MPLS and does not support PREOF, requiring only one path per flow. Protocol extensions would be limited, primarily to existing IP routing protocols.

Segment Routing (either SR-MPLS or SRv6) offers another approach, where paths are encoded directly in packet headers as a list of segments. This reduces signaling overhead and node state compared to legacy MPLS, which is beneficial for DetNet because large numbers of flows may need to be established.
sections.plainLanguage: The controller works with different types of networks—some use labels, some use IP addresses, and some use path instructions in the packet itself.

sections.title: Monitoring and Operations
sections.content:
The management plane must monitor DetNet flow performance to ensure flows meet their SLA requirements. Active performance monitoring injects test traffic into the network, but this adds extra load and is not recommended for operational DetNet domains—it is useful only for commissioning or troubleshooting.

Passive performance monitoring, such as In Situ Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (IOAM), monitors actual service traffic without injecting extra traffic. This is the preferred approach for DetNet. The management plane must also support connectivity verification and fault management to detect when links or nodes fail and trigger recovery mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: The controller watches the network to make sure everything is working. It can either send test messages or watch real messages go by, and it fixes problems when it spots them.
